WalkthroughText: Array algorithms like finding the min/max, summing, counting, and reversing all follow the same pattern: you walk through the array index by index with a loop, and you keep a running "tracker" variable in memory that updates based on what you see at each index. The indexedStrip shows the array's boxes and the current index pointer, while a memCell shows the tracker variable (like max, sum, or count) changing value as the loop progresses. Reversing is slightly different — instead of tracking one running value, you swap pairs of elements using a temporary memCell, working from both ends toward the middle. Watching the index pointer move alongside the memCell values is the key to understanding why these algorithms work correctly.

Choices: It will return an incorrect result if all elements in arr are negative.
It will throw an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for any non-empty array.
It will return 0 whenever the array is empty, which is correct in every case.
It fails to update max correctly when arr[i] equals max.
PracticeItems.Explanation: Initializing max to 0 fails when every element is negative, because no element will ever be greater than 0, so max incorrectly stays 0 instead of becoming the true (negative) maximum. The loop bounds are correct (i < arr.length), so no exception occurs. The equal-value case is irrelevant since the condition only needs to trigger on strictly greater values, which it does correctly.

Choices: It counts even elements; count starts at 0 because no evens have been found yet before the loop begins.
It counts odd elements; count starts at 0 because Java requires all int variables to start at 0.
It sums the even elements; count starts at 0 to avoid adding an initial garbage value.
It counts even elements; count must start at 0 or the loop will not execute at all.
PracticeItems.Explanation: count is an accumulator that tallies how many times arr[i] % 2 == 0 is true, so it must start at 0 to represent 'zero evens found so far' before any elements are examined. It has nothing to do with sums, and Java does not require int variables to be zero-initialized (local variables must be explicitly initialized) — the loop's execution doesn't depend on count's starting value.

Choices: Using i < arr.length / 2 stops the loop after each pair of elements has been swapped once, preventing the elements from being swapped back to their original order.
Using i < arr.length / 2 is required because arrays in Java can only be traversed halfway before causing an error.
Using i < arr.length / 2 makes the method run in constant time instead of linear time.
Using i < arr.length / 2 ensures temp is not overwritten before its value is used.
PracticeItems.Explanation: Each iteration swaps a pair of elements (one from the front, one from the back), so only half of the array's length worth of iterations are needed; continuing past the midpoint would swap each pair back to its original positions, undoing the reversal. There's no such restriction on array traversal in Java, and the loop bound doesn't affect time complexity in the way described (it's still O(n) overall) or protect temp's value, which is protected simply by using a local variable correctly.

WalkthroughSteps.Caption: Let's trace findMax on the array {3, 7, 2, 9, 5}. We start by creating the array on our indexedStrip.
We set up the method's stack frame and initialize max to the first element's value... wait, actually this version initializes max to 0, so let's watch what happens.
We also create the loop counter i, starting at 0, and highlight the loop line.
At index 0, arr[0] is 3. We compare 3 to max (0): since 3 > 0 is true, max updates to 3.
We move the index pointer to 1. arr[1] is 7. Since 7 > 3 is true, max updates to 7.
Index moves to 2. arr[2] is 2. Since 2 > 7 is false, max stays at 7 — no update happens.
Index moves to 3. arr[3] is 9. Since 9 > 7 is true, max updates to 9, the new running maximum.
Index moves to 4, the last index. arr[4] is 5. Since 5 > 9 is false, max stays at 9.
The loop ends because i would become 5, which is not less than arr.length. We return the final value of max, which is 9 — the correct maximum of the array.

Notice the pattern: at every index, we compared the current element to our tracker (max) and updated it only when the new element was larger — this same 'index + tracker' pattern works for sum (add every element) and count (increment when a condition is true).
